name: Coalition for Rainforest Nations (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the forest's carbon, the buyers' extra emissions and the pandemic risk forest loss carries all reach the whole world, spread by world population.
summary: The Coalition for Rainforest Nations helps rainforest countries in the UN climate talks, trains their teams to measure and report their forest results so they can be paid for cutting deforestation, and helps them sell forest carbon credits under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. We model all of its 2024 programme spending ($4.0 million) in three branches: the forest kept by donors' results-based payments; the forest kept by credit sales, less the extra emissions of buyers who count the credits against their own targets; and the climate-finance goal agreed at COP29, its adaptation money valued as aid and its mitigation money in tonnes. The result is a small net harm, close to zero, and nearly all of it is the finance goal: some climate finance is aid moved from health, education and other development work into mitigation, which is worth far less in healthy years, and at the best guesses the aid lost slightly outweighs the new adaptation aid and the mitigation gained, with its cleaner air. The share of the goal's money that is new aid decides the sign: at about half new the result is zero, and above it positive. The forest branches rest on one evaluation, Norway's payments to Guyana, credit CfRN with its small share of all the money behind the forest kept, and are small; the credit sales are a small net harm. Every branch takes the missing-data discount, and the result is mostly uncertainty: in the simulation it is harmful in about three draws of five.

rows.explainer: Everything the Coalition for Rainforest Nations (CfRN) spent on its one reported programme in 2024, the latest year filed: REDD+ (reducing emissions from deforestation and forest degradation), its "ongoing flagship program" (Part III). The return says the statements were not audited or reviewed by an accountant (Part XII line 2), so the Form 990 is the accounts. Its 2024 Annual Impact Statement describes three pillars inside that programme: the UN climate negotiations, national implementation (carbon-market laws, registries and sales) and data collection and capacity building. All three are modelled below, as three branches: forest kept by donors' results-based payments, forest kept by credit sales under Article 6 net of buyers' extra emissions, and the climate-finance goal (rbf_share_of_programme, fin_share_of_programme).

rows.explainer: Contractors who train government forestry teams as staff would (Convention 1 counts them with staff). The other professional fees ($1,336,316: legal, registry and communications work) are left out: firms paid market rates, with no forgone pay.

rows.label: Share of the programme on measuring forest results for results-based payments
rows.explainer: CfRN reports no split of its one programme. Our judgment: 45% (30-60%) goes to work that lets rainforest countries measure, report and have verified their forest results and claim results-based payments from donors (the rbf branch): training and data collection with 15 countries in 2024 (forest reference levels, greenhouse-gas inventories, biennial reports; the forestry experts' $631,375 in Schedule O) and the negotiations on REDD+ finance. A tenth goes to the climate-finance goal (fin_share_of_programme). The rest goes to the carbon markets of Article 6 of the Paris Agreement (the itmo branch): negotiating its rules, completed at COP29 in 2024, and national implementation in four countries (carbon-market laws, registries, readying Suriname's credits for sale), which the 2024 Impact Statement gives as much space. Anchor: the statement's own weight among its pillars; travel and meetings ($522,448) serve all three.

rows.label: Share of the programme on the negotiations for the climate-finance goal
rows.explainer: The finance goal was one of the two COP29 results CfRN's Impact Statement leads with, but one strand of its negotiations work beside REDD+ and Article 6, which take its data, legal and implementation teams. Our judgment a tenth (3-20%) of the programme.

rows.explainer: The new collective quantified goal: developed countries to provide or mobilise $300 billion a year for developing countries by 2035.

rows.label: The $100 billion goal it replaces

source.title: Coalition for Rainforest Nations, Annual Impact Statement 2024
source.quote: all countries had agreed to triple climate finance for developing countries from $100 to $300 billion annually by 2035

rows.explainer: The goal set in 2009 for 2020, which the new goal triples.

rows.label: Share of the rise in climate finance that the goal itself causes
rows.explainer: Climate finance was rising before the goal and would go on rising with development banks' plans and donors' budgets; a goal adds pressure and a yardstick, but nothing binds a donor. Anchor: the $100 billion goal, due by 2020, was reached only in 2022, two years late, at $115.9 billion (OECD, reported by Clean Energy Wire), so goals of this kind are met late and largely by finance that was coming anyway. Our judgment: 15% of the $200 billion rise is the goal's own doing (3-40%). Whether it is delivered at all is fin_implementation_adj; whether the goal itself would have been agreed anyway is fin_counterfactual_adj.

rows.label: Share of the goal's finance worth as much as a grant
rows.explainer: The goal counts loans at face value and private money mobilised; a loan repaid is worth only its subsidy to the borrower, and a project financed by a market-rate loan would often have been financed anyway. Anchor: of the $115.9 billion of 2022, "most of it is provided as loans" (Oxfam's Jan Kowalzig, in Clean Energy Wire's report of OECD's figures). Our judgment 40% (20-70%), the grant-equivalent part. Applied to both the aid's value and the mitigation tonnes: only the subsidy decides whether a project happens.

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: share of the money for adaptation and cross-cutting aid
rows.explainer: In 2022 "less than one third" of climate finance went to adapting to climate change and "most" to mitigation (OECD, reported by Clean Energy Wire); cross-cutting projects (both at once) are valued with adaptation as aid. Our judgment 35% (25-50%). The rest, mitigation, is counted in tonnes (fin_mitigation_tco2e_per_year), as the site counts every mitigation (docs/normalization.md 2.20: aid whose use is known is valued at that use's figure).

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: share of the money that is new aid, not diverted from other aid
rows.explainer: Much public climate finance is development aid relabelled or moved from health, education and other aid. CARE's Seeing Double (2023, p. 4): "only 7 per cent of the climate finance provided from 2011 to 2020 is found to be new and additional" to donors' aid commitments, and under the weak definition 52% is development finance diverted (https://care.dk/media/ckjh2s3p/seeing-double-2023.pdf). Our judgment 40% new (7-70%), between Seeing Double's two definitions. The diverted money loses the value of the aid it replaced (docs/normalization.md 2.20: aid displaced counts).

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: value of a dollar of aid
rows.explainer: The site's shared figure for a donor's aid budget (docs/normalization.md 2.20), for the adaptation aid gained and the other aid displaced alike.

rows.label: Value lost per dollar of rich donor countries' public money, units of value
rows.explainer: What a dollar of a donor government's money costs its taxpayers (docs/normalization.md 2.23): the shared cost of raising public funds (facts: public_funds.mcpf) over taxpayers' consumption on the survey scale, at the site's European figure (UK consumption per person × its survey ratio, 2.14) for the donors (Norway, Germany, the Green Climate Fund's contributors, Japan, Switzerland), with the US federal payer multiple as the shared stand-in for how a national tax falls (our judgment: no other country's figure is shared yet).

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: prices in 2035 against 2024
rows.explainer: The goal is in dollars of the day, not indexed, and the model counts in 2024 dollars (Convention 8). Anchor: the Federal Reserve's and the ECB's 2% inflation targets over eleven years, 1.02^11 = 1.24 (1.15-1.40). No shared inflation forecast exists in facts/.

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: grant-equivalent finance it adds a year at the 2035 level, in 2024 dollars
Climate-finance goal: share of the money that isn't new whose use is unchanged (rebadged)
rows.explainer: Money that fails CARE's test of new aid isn't all aid moved to new uses: CARE calls much of it development finance "rebadged" with climate objectives (Seeing Double 2023, p. 7), and its p. 6 cites studies finding that donors over-report the climate relevance of their projects. Rebadged money neither loses an aid project nor builds a mitigation project: its value is zero. Our judgment 40% (20-70%) of the money that isn't new.

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: value as aid a year, net of the aid displaced and of what the new money costs its payers
rows.formula: fin_grant_dollars_per_year * fin_value_per_dollar * (fin_adaptation_share * fin_new_aid_share - (1 - fin_adaptation_share) * (1 - fin_new_aid_share) * (1 - fin_rebadged_share)) - fin_grant_dollars_per_year * fin_new_aid_share * donor_payer_uov_per_dollar
rows.explainer: New money for adaptation adds the value of aid; money moved to adaptation from other aid nets to nothing (aid for aid); money moved to mitigation loses the aid it replaced, and its tonnes are counted separately; rebadged money changes nothing. Negative when the money moved to mitigation outweighs the new adaptation money. New money also costs the donors' taxpayers (row donor_payer_uov_per_dollar, docs/normalization.md 2.23); money moved from other aid costs them nothing more.

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: grant-equivalent finance per tonne of CO₂e its mitigation projects avoid over their lives
rows.explainer: Anchor on the row's own basis: the Green Climate Fund's 286 projects "are expected to abate a total of 3.1 billion tonnes" over their lives, and its allocation "stands in grant equivalent terms at ... 44 per cent (USD 4.3 billion) for mitigation" (GCF report to COP29, UNFCCC FCCC/CP/2024/3, p. 3, https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/resource/cp2024_03a01.pdf): about $1.4 a tonne of grant-equivalent GCF money, about $3.4 with the co-financing counted at a quarter of its face value. Those are the accredited entities' own ex-ante estimates; projections of this kind run ahead of what is built and claim cuts that would have come anyway (families/climate.md), so our judgment is about three times the ex-ante figure (the $3.4 counts the $45.6 billion of co-financing at a quarter, split like GCF money with 54% to mitigation: $4.3 billion + 0.54 × 0.25 × $45.6 billion ≈ $10.5 billion over 3.1 billion tonnes; the haircut is our judgment, not a published evaluation), $10 ($3-40, from no haircut to ten times).

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: CO₂e its added mitigation finance avoids over the projects' lives, per year of finance at the 2035 level
rows.explainer: New and moved mitigation money alike build projects; rebadged money builds nothing new.

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: years over which a mitigation project's tonnes come
rows.explainer: The cost per tonne buys a project's lifetime tonnes, which come over its years of use and are discounted (the climate family's direct cuts). Anchor: energy access and power generation take "the largest portion of GCF funding (39 per cent)" of its mitigation (GCF report, p. 3); power plants and grids run 20-30 years, efficiency and transport projects less. 20 years (10-30).

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: air pollution its mitigation tonnes carry, relative to an average fossil-fuel tonne
rows.explainer: Anchor: energy and power take about two fifths of mitigation finance (GCF report, p. 3: 39%), and low-emission transport much of the rest; in developing countries the power displaced is largely coal and diesel without scrubbers, whose smoke per tonne is at or above the world fossil average the shared rate is built on; forests and farming carry no fuel smoke. Our judgment half the world fossil-fuel average (10-120%).

rows.explainer: The assessment's own average: $24.5 billion at $2.4 billion a year is about ten years, 2010 to about 2020 (published February 2022). It cancels out of the result (rbp_per_year scales the tonnes and CfRN's share alike).

rows.label: Results-based payments a year, all REDD+ countries
rows.explainer: About $460 million a year. Commitments, not disbursements: some is paid years later or never (the shortfall sits in rbp_evidence_adj; the attribution row divides by commitments too).

rows.label: Readiness and implementation support per dollar of results-based payments
rows.explainer: Grants for the kind of work CfRN does (forest monitoring, reference levels, REDD+ strategies) over the payments for results: about $0.39 of support per dollar paid. The base of CfRN's share in both forest branches: the payers and the forest countries' own budgets, which carry out the protection, are under the mobiliser's share.

rows.label: Carbon markets: money paid a year for rainforest countries' forest credits under Article 6, once the market works
rows.explainer: No forest credit had been transferred under Article 6 by the end of 2024: Suriname announced the world's first sale of such credits (Impact Statement 2024, p. 4) and expected it in 2025. Anchors: Hess's purchase of Guyana's jurisdictional credits, at least $750 million over 2022-2032, about $75 million a year for one country; all donors' results-based payments, about $460 million a year. Our judgment: $200 million a year ($50 million to $1 billion). It cancels out of the result: CfRN's share of the resources falls as the market grows (itmo_attribution_share).

rows.label: Carbon markets: price of a forest credit (a tonne of reduced emissions)

source.title: Stabroek News (11 January 2023), Hess makes US$75M first payment for Guyana-issued carbon credits
source.quote: US$37.5 million for 2.5 million ART-TREES credits from 2016 at a price of US$15/tonne of CO2e

rows.explainer: Hess's deal with Guyana, the largest sale of a country's forest credits so far, is worth at least $750 million between 2022 and 2032; its first payment priced the 2016 and 2017 credits at $15 a tonne, and later vintages are priced higher. Our estimate $15 ($10-30), the quoted price: $10 is the low end of jurisdictional forest credits, $30 a price only the best-rated units reach.

Tropical forest in the countries working under the UN's REDD+ framework

source.title: Coalition for Rainforest Nations, Annual Impact Statement 2024

The hectares kept a year are rbf_ha_per_year and itmo_ha_per_year.

rows.label: Results-based payments per tonne of CO₂ kept out of the air, Guyana 2010-2015 (dollars of the time)

source.title: Roopsind, Sohngen and Brandt (2019), Evidence that a national REDD+ program reduces tree cover loss and carbon emissions in a high forest cover, low deforestation country, PNAS 116(49): 24492-24499
source.quote: Based on assumed payments of US$250 million, the cost of the 12.8 million tons of avoided CO2 emissions is US$19.53 per ton of CO2.

rows.explainer: The one quasi-experimental evaluation of a national results-based REDD+ programme: Norway's offer of $250 million to Guyana for keeping deforestation low in 2010-2015 cut tree-cover loss by 35% against a synthetic control, 12.8 million tonnes of CO₂, $19.53 a tonne if the loss avoided is permanent (that question is permanence_share). The paper reports bootstrapped 95% intervals only in its appendix; the range, $12 to $40, is ours, wider on the high side because Guyana's reference level was set high and other countries' programmes may buy less.

rows.label: Years of the Norway-Guyana payments (2010-2015)

source.title: Roopsind, Sohngen and Brandt (2019), Evidence that a national REDD+ program reduces tree cover loss and carbon emissions in a high forest cover, low deforestation country, PNAS 116(49): 24492-24499
source.quote: with Norway offering to pay US$250 million to Guyana if annual deforestation rates remained below 0.056% from 2010 to 2015.

rows.explainer: Six years, 2010 to 2015: the payments' price level is the average of those years'.

rows.label: Results-based payments per tonne of CO₂ kept out of the air, in 2024 dollars
rows.explainer: Guyana's cost per tonne in 2024 prices (× US consumer prices in 2024 over their 2010-2015 average, about 1.36: Convention 8), so that it divides 2024 dollars of payments, credit sales and CfRN's spending alike: about $26.65.

rows.label: Share of the forest kept that stays standing for good
rows.explainer: Tree-cover loss in Guyana rose after the payments ended (Roopsind et al. 2019: "without continued payments, forest protection is not guaranteed"), so some forest kept is only cleared later. Our judgment half (20-90%).

rows.label: Share of the clearing avoided that moves elsewhere
rows.explainer: A country paid to clear less may push clearing (gold mining, farming, logging) across the border; Roopsind et al. flag leakage as possible but unmeasured. Our judgment 20% (0-50%), as for the leakage rows of The Nature Conservancy's forest branches. Failure of the main effect, so it stays in the main chain, not among side effects.

rows.label: How far Guyana's result holds for the payments CfRN's countries get
rows.explainer: Guyana's is one country, with low deforestation and a forward-looking contract that rewarded each year's restraint. Most of the money CfRN helps countries claim pays for results years after the fact (Honduras's 2016-2020 results were verified in 2024), which rewards the past more than it changes the future, and reference levels set high pay for reductions that would have come anyway. Our judgment 0.5 (0.2-1), anchored on The Nature Conservancy's 0.4-0.75 for forest rules judged from other places' studies. Used for both branches' forest tonnes.

rows.label: CO₂ released per hectare of tropical forest lost
rows.explainer: The tropics' average, 2.4 billion tonnes over 3.7 million hectares lost in 2023 (about {{row:tco2_per_ha_lost}} tonnes a hectare; World Resources Institute, the shared figures every forest model reads). Only used to turn tonnes into hectares for the pandemic-risk rows.

rows.label: CO₂ kept out of the air a year by all the finance, per hectare of REDD+ forest
rows.explainer: For reading only: the forest carbon the donors' payments and the credit sales keep a year (before CfRN's share), spread over the 1.6 billion hectares under REDD+. Nothing on the path reads it.

rows.label: Years of forest kept that a year's work counts
rows.explainer: One, for the two forest branches (the finance goal counts its own won years, fin_years): both set a year of CfRN's spending against a year of the finance flows it shares in, with CfRN credited its share of that year's resources (an ongoing flow counts one year against one year's cost, Convention 3). The new Article 6 rules are part of the stock of rules and institutions every year's flow rests on, which is why the flow, not the rule, is counted.

rows.label: Years from the year's work until the forest is kept
rows.explainer: Countries CfRN helps report in one year and are paid a year or more later (Honduras's results verified in 2024, its first sales planned for 2025); Article 6's first forest credits were due on the market in 2025-2027. The forest kept follows the expectation of payment, so about two years (half a year to four). Discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Years of forest kept, discounted
Results-based finance: CO₂ kept out of the air a year by all donors' payments, for good
rows.explainer: The year's payments over the cost per tonne, × the share that stays standing, × the share not displaced. How far Guyana's result holds is the branch's evidence adjustment.

rows.label: Results-based finance: CO₂ kept, discounted years
Results-based finance: tropical forest kept a year
Carbon markets: CO₂ kept out of the air a year by the money buyers pay
rows.explainer: The same chain as results-based payments: money paid for results keeps forest standing at Guyana's cost per tonne, × permanence, × leakage, × how far Guyana's result holds (applied here, not in the branch's evidence row, so it doesn't shrink the buyers' extra emissions below as well).

rows.label: Carbon markets: share of the credits bought by countries for their own targets
rows.explainer: Article 6 credits go to countries counting them against their national pledges (Switzerland, Sweden, Japan, Singapore's government), to airlines under CORSIA, to companies under carbon taxes that accept them (Singapore's), and to companies buying voluntarily (CfRN's REDD.plus platform). CfRN's own plan is purchases "by corporations and sovereign governments", possibly through a carbon tax like Singapore's (Impact Statement 2024, p. 32). Our judgment: half to countries (20-80%).

rows.label: Carbon markets: share of countries' credits that replace cuts they would otherwise make
rows.explainer: A country that counts a forest credit against its own target can cut a tonne less at home. If the credit is a real extra tonne kept, the two cancel; if not, the world emits more. The real tonnes are itmo_forest_tco2e_per_year; this row is how many of countries' credits replace cuts they would otherwise have made. A country that would have met its target anyway replaces cuts one for one; one that would have missed it (CfRN: the credits "help developed countries who fail to hit their climate pledges") replaces fewer. Our judgment half (20-90%). The failure of the market's main chain (credits for reductions that would have happened anyway), so it is in the main chain, not a side effect.

rows.label: Carbon markets: real cuts in the units other buyers would otherwise have bought
rows.explainer: An airline under CORSIA or a company buying voluntarily would otherwise have bought another credit; a company under a carbon tax would otherwise have paid the tax. So a forest credit they buy instead loses only the real cut in the unit it displaced, and none where the tax would have been paid. A blend: Probst et al. (2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11564741/) estimate that "less than 16%" of credits issued are real cuts (25% for avoided deforestation), an upper bound, × the three quarters of these buyers we judge buy instead of another credit rather than instead of a tax. 12% (0-30%), no fuel smoke: the displaced units are mostly other offsets.

rows.label: Carbon markets: extra fossil emissions by country buyers a year
Carbon markets: extra emissions a year from all buyers
rows.explainer: Countries' forgone cuts at home, plus the real cuts lost in the units other buyers would otherwise have bought.

rows.label: Carbon markets: CO₂ kept a year, net of buyers' extra emissions
rows.explainer: Negative when the buyers' extra emissions exceed the real tonnes the money keeps: at the best guesses each credit sold at $15 keeps about a tenth of a tonne of forest carbon (Probst et al. 2024 find a quarter of avoided-deforestation credits real, a cross-check) and lets buyers emit about three tenths of a tonne more.

rows.label: Carbon markets: net CO₂, discounted years

rows.explainer: The land-use share of new diseases × the share of it that scales with tropical forest loss × the yearly chance of a COVID-scale pandemic, per hectare of the tropics' yearly loss: the risk falls in proportion to the forest kept. The least grounded number here.

Carbon markets: fall in the yearly pandemic chance × discounted years

rows.explainer: The shared judgment for a COVID-scale pandemic: about 15% of adult excess deaths were under 50; the rest are valued at the 50-74 band.

rows.explainer: A catastrophe's deaths are valued like every death on the site, by age band × your value of a life; no premium for their number.

Results-based finance: what the donors' payments cost their taxpayers, units of value (negative)
rows.explainer: Public money that buys tonnes is netted against what it costs those who pay for it (docs/normalization.md 2.23): the year's payments × the value lost per dollar, over the same discounted years as the forest kept; credited with the branch (in uov_bridged), all but its evidence step, which is about the tonnes.

rows.label: Carbon markets: what governments' purchases of credits cost their taxpayers, units of value (negative)
rows.explainer: The credits bought by countries for their own targets are bought with public money (docs/normalization.md 2.23); companies' purchases are their own money, as any private purchase. Over the same discounted years as the forest kept, credited with the branch.

Catastrophic risk: fall in the yearly pandemic chance from the year's work
rows.explainer: For reading: the forest each branch keeps × its credit × the risk per hectare.

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: share of the win due to all its advocates
rows.explainer: The goal is agreed, so the chance is the shared share of a won climate policy due to all advocates together, rather than to governments, events and opinion (facts/climate.json, {{row:fin_p_success}}, 10-60%); CfRN's part of the advocates is fin_attribution_share.

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: years of negotiation behind it
rows.explainer: The talks on the new goal ran from the decision at COP26 (2021) to its adoption at COP29 (2024), about three years (2-5). As a past average, a year's spending gets one year's share of the win (Convention 11).

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: years until the added finance flows at the goal's level
rows.explainer: The goal's level is "by 2035", eleven years after 2024; the money counted is that level, so the wait is to 2035 (8-14: some of it sooner, some later than the goal). Discounted at the shared rate (normalization.md 2.9).

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: discounted years counted
rows.explainer: The site's years a won reform counts ($win_years_counted, normalization.md 2.9), after the wait, discounted.

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: value of the finance added, one year's share of the win
rows.explainer: The value of the finance the goal adds a year, net of aid displaced, × the advocates' share of the win × the discounted years counted ÷ the years of negotiation. Compliance costs (normalization.md 2.21): none counted beyond the aid displaced, since the goal binds no payer and new aid is valued as aid won is everywhere on the site.

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: mitigation tonnes, one year's share of the win, before waits and years counted
rows.explainer: Used to weight the smoke these tonnes carry (air_pollution_weight), which may read no shared value.

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: mitigation tonnes, one year's share of the win, discounted years
rows.explainer: The tonnes × the discounted years counted (from 2035) × the projects' tonnes spread over their lives, discounted (section 2: every future benefit is discounted). The smoke weight (fin_mitigation_tco2e_pre_wait) leaves the discounting out, since a conversion row reads no shared value.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: share of every later year's healthy life the catastrophe would take
rows.explainer: The shared judgment: 0, the world recovers from a COVID-scale pandemic; its deaths are counted above.

rows.label: Discounted future years of healthy life per person of the long-run population, if the future ends now
rows.explainer: The site's one count of future generations (docs/normalization.md 2.19): the healthy years of people not yet born, discounted for ever at the shared rate. People alive now die in the catastrophe and are counted as deaths, so this stream rises from nothing to the long-run population over one lifetime (@catastrophe.life_expectancy_now) and then runs on: about 8 years at the default 4%, about 960 at the 0.1% floor. Fixed; don't edit.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: future generations' healthy years
rows.explainer: 0 at the best guess (future_share_lost); credited by branch.

rows.label: Suffering of the farmed animals the people of that future would eat, in healthy years
rows.explainer: A future kept is also every animal raised to feed it: each future person-year at the suffering of the animals an average person eats in a year today (docs/normalization.md 2.25). Suffering always counts, whatever lives that never start count; the farmed animals' own good days count where you set them to. Held at today's diet: no forecast of what people will eat is used.

rows.label: Results-based finance: share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Whether the payments would have reached the countries without outside support at all: donors and forest governments had their own reasons to strike these deals. No study splits it; the reference class is the site's shared figure for the part of a won climate policy that is due to outside groups at all (facts: climate.advocacy_share_of_policy_win, 30%, 10% to 60%; Burstein & Linton 2002). The forest that would have stood anyway is already out of the cost per tonne (a synthetic control).

rows.label: Results-based finance: CfRN's share of the support behind the payments
rows.explainer: CfRN's spending on this branch over all the readiness and implementation support a year that lets countries measure, report and claim payments (Forest Declaration Assessment 2022: $1.8 billion over ten years beside $4.6 billion of payments), the work done alongside it: under 1%. The donors who pay and the governments that do the protecting are under the mobiliser's share, not in this denominator. Measured over all REDD+ countries, which scales the tonnes alike.

rows.label: Results-based finance: share of credit used
rows.explainer: The share among those who paid for or did the same work, times the mobiliser's share: the rest of the credit stays with those who carry out or adopt the result (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: Results-based finance: delivery
rows.explainer: 1: money committed but not paid lowers the payments and the resources alike, and payments for old results are in the evidence row.

rows.label: Results-based finance: discount for outcomes not measured
rows.explainer: Thin: neither CfRN nor its countries measure the forest its work keeps; the branch rests on one evaluation in Guyana and judgment (Convention 12).

rows.label: Results-based finance: adjustments that read no shared value
rows.explainer: Split out so the share of fossil tonnes (fuel_share) can be weighted by branch without reading a shared value; the missing-data discount and next-dollar factor are the same for both forest branches.

Results-based finance: credit

CfRN is one of many negotiating parties and groups on Article 6; that is inside this share.

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: share of the rise in the goal that wasn't coming anyway
rows.explainer: A new goal was due anyway: the Paris decision (1/CP.21, para. 53) required one before 2025 "from a floor of USD 100 billion per year", and the COP29 presidency's draft of 22 November 2024 already proposed $250 billion a year, raised to $300 billion the next day (UN News, 22 November 2024, https://news.un.org/en/story/2024/11/1157346). Our judgment: half the rise from $100 billion to $300 billion wasn't coming anyway (25%, only the last step from the draft, to 80%). Whether the finance follows the goal is fin_added_by_goal_share; the advocates' part of what was won is fin_p_success.

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: all advocates' and negotiation-support groups' resources on it a year
rows.explainer: The same kind of resource and the same groups as fin_p_success (advocates, not governments): the research, campaign and negotiation-support groups that worked on the finance goal (climate-finance think tanks, development and environment NGOs and their networks, groups backing developing-country blocs, CfRN among them). Our judgment, a rough count without a published tally: about 50 groups at $0.5-3 million a year each on this item, about $80 million, with a wide range ($20-300 million) because the count is ours. Government delegations are left out: they are what fin_p_success already sets aside.

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: CfRN's share of all advocates' resources on it
rows.explainer: CfRN's spending on the finance talks over all advocates' resources on them (Convention 2): about half a percent at the best guesses.

rows.label: This charity's share of the good done with money, work or budgets it brings in
rows.explainer: The site's one setting for resources another party commits only because of the organisation (docs/normalization.md 2.24): governments' budgets and enforcement, companies' compliance, the use others make of research. The charity is credited this share of the good done with them, net of their cost; the rest stays with those who paid or did the work. Fixed.

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: share of credit used
rows.explainer: The share among those who paid for or did the same work, times the mobiliser's share: the rest of the credit stays with those who carry out or adopt the result (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: share of the goal's added finance delivered
rows.explainer: Nothing binds a donor to the goal; the largest, the US, left the Paris Agreement in 2025, and aid budgets in Europe are being cut. Anchor: the $100 billion goal was met, but two years late (OECD, reported by Clean Energy Wire), and in a time of growing aid budgets. Our judgment half (20-90%).

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: 1: the payers' money is already in each branch's share of the resources. Below 1 if CfRN's funders would otherwise fund similar REDD+ support; above 1 if its help brings in money that wouldn't go to forests at all. Range 0.85-1.1. Applied to all branches.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of the result
rows.explainer: Positive: the integrity rules CfRN pressed for in Article 6 (reviews that flag inconsistent credits), and greenhouse-gas inventories that countries also use for their national climate pledges. Negative: donors may shift money from results-based grants to buying credits they count against their own targets. Net 0 (−20% to +20%), as a share of the result's size (outcome_total), so its good end adds good and its harmful end adds harm whatever the result's sign.

rows.explainer: Forest carbon carries no fuel smoke; country buyers' extra emissions do, and they are negative tonnes in the total, so their share is negative. Weighted by tonnes before waits and years counted, as the climate family does (a conversion row reads no shared value): the finance goal's tonnes come later and count more years than the forest's, so the smoke is split between the two sources approximately, not exactly.

rows.explainer: Buyers of forest credits are rich countries (Switzerland, Singapore, Japan, Sweden) and airlines under CORSIA, whose forgone cuts are in power plants with scrubbers, vehicles and jet fuel burnt mostly at altitude. Anchors: the site's shared factors for US power (0.013), US vehicles (0.04) and California's cap-and-invest (0.07); jet fuel at altitude adds little ground-level smoke. Our judgment 0.025 (0.01-0.14).
